analysis.one_liner: Requires 60-day advance notice for multi-site mass layoffs and doubles the penalty for skipping it.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee in April 2009, sent to a subcommittee in June, and never received a vote before the 111th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification (WARN) Act already requires employers to give 60 days' notice before a big single-site plant closing or layoff. This bill would close a gap: employers could no longer dodge the notice requirement by spreading one big layoff across multiple sites, and it would raise the penalty for violating the law from back pay alone to double back pay. It never advanced past a House subcommittee.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at large companies that conduct layoffs spread across several sites would get 60 days' written notice, giving them time to look for other work, arrange training, or file for unemployment, and any employer that skipped the notice would owe affected workers twice their lost pay for up to 60 days. State and local officials would also get notice, letting governments prepare for sudden local job losses.

how_it_helps.text: The bill adds a new trigger to the WARN Act covering a single employer cutting at least 33% of its workforce (and at least 50 workers), or at least 500 workers, when the job losses happen at more than one site within a 30-day period. Employers could no longer split one large layoff into several smaller site-level notices to stay under the thresholds.

It raises the penalty for violating the notice requirement from back pay alone to two times the amount of back pay for each day of violation, up to 60 days, giving workers who lose the notice period twice the compensation they would otherwise recover.
Notice would also go to state and local government officials for multi-site mass layoffs, letting governments respond to sudden local job losses.

analysis.who_pays: Large employers that conduct multi-site mass layoffs would bear new compliance costs — preparing and delivering 60-day notices for each affected site — and would face double back pay liability if they violate the law. Companies that currently structure layoffs site-by-site to avoid the WARN thresholds would lose that option.

drawbacks.text: Doubling the damages raises the cost of any violation roughly two-fold, and employers argue that stiffer penalties on top of broader coverage add to the cost of restructuring, which can fall back on workers and communities if companies respond by cutting jobs sooner, moving work offshore, or using contractors and spin-offs that fall outside the WARN Act's reach.

The bill's multi-site trigger is mechanical: any single employer with job losses at more than one site hitting the 33%-and-50-worker or 500-worker thresholds within a 30-day window would be covered, which could sweep in retail chains and other multi-location employers whose site-level cuts were not part of a coordinated layoff, adding notice obligations in cases where advance warning is hard to predict.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but narrow: it protects workers at large multi-site layoffs, a gap that became visible during mass retail and service-sector closures, and doubling damages gives the notice requirement teeth it otherwise lacks. The costs fall only on large employers planning such layoffs, though honest supporters would concede that harsher penalties and broader triggers can push some restructuring into forms that dodge the law entirely, and the bill does nothing to fix those workarounds.

outcome.mechanism: The House committee it was referred to sent it to a subcommittee in June 2009, and it never came back out for a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 23, 2009 and referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and Labor.

On June 4, 2009, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections, which is where the action record ends; no markup, floor vote, or further movement is recorded before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.
The bill never received a roll-call vote in either chamber, so no member ever had to vote for or against it on the merits.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that conduct multi-site mass layoffs are better off, since the multi-site notice requirement and doubled penalties never became law; workers who would have gained notice and double back pay got nothing.

for.name: Rep. Luis Gutierrez
for.role: Sponsor; Chair of the Subcommittee on Immigration
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on April 23, 2009 and delivered introductory remarks on the floor.

for.name: 10 of 253 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Sponsored and cosponsored the bill; no Democrat other than these ten signed on, and no Republican did.

against.name: House Committee on Education and Labor
against.role: Committee of referral (chair: Rep. George Miller, D-CA)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral, sent it to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections, and never reported it out or scheduled it for action during the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had ten Democratic backers and no recorded Republican support, but it never reached a vote, so no party split was ever recorded on the merits.

industries.industry: Large multi-site employers (retail chains, manufacturers, service companies)
industries.note: These employers would face a new 60-day notice obligation for multi-site mass layoffs and double back pay for violations, closing the workaround of splitting layoffs across sites. Their interest in the bill's failure ran directly against workers' interest in getting notice and compensation.
